Coaxal Circles

GeometryCirclesAlgebra
Game: This is a picture, not a game: it shows two families of circles that cross each other at right angles.
How to play: Drag A or B along the line, or focus one and use the arrow keys. Change N, tick Family 1 or Family 2, and press Reset to put the points back.
Look for the math

Move A and B and the picture changes, but the two families keep meeting at right angles. The old applet drew this with a green and an orange gradient; here each family has one clear colour so the pattern is easier to see.

Two families of circles

Let the midpoint of AB be X and let s = AB/2. The first family puts a centre t units from X along the line AB, with radius √(t² − s²); since t starts at s + 10, no centre lies between A and B. These are the Apollonian circles, and they nest without crossing. The second family puts a centre u units from X on the perpendicular bisector, with radius √(u² + s²), plus the circle on AB as diameter. Every one of those circles passes through both A and B. The logic test compares all of these numbers with a fresh transcription of the applet's own loops for 252 settings of A, B and N.

One shared radical axis

For a first-family circle, the power of a point (X, y) on the upright line is s² + (y − y₀)² — the same number for every t. For a second-family circle, the power of a point (x, y₀) on the line AB is (x − X)² − s² — the same for every u. So any two circles in a family share the same radical axis: the upright line for the first family, the line AB for the second. That shared axis is why they are called coaxal. As a circle of the first family grows, its arc beside X settles onto that upright line: the straight-line member of the family is the perpendicular bisector of AB.

Why the crossings are square

Take a circle with parameter t from the first family and one with u from the second. Their centres are √(t² + u²) apart, while the squares of their radii add to (t² − s²) + (u² + s²) = t² + u². Since centre distance squared equals the sum of the radii squared, the circles are orthogonal. The same calculation works for the circle on AB as diameter (u = 0). The article's other half says that two pencils of circles tangent at one point are orthogonal too when their axes are the two perpendicular lines through that point: their centres are t and u from the point, so the same sum of squares applies. The article proves the first half by inversion in a circle centred at A: the circles through A and B become straight lines through one point, the Apollonian circles become circles centred at that point, and inversion keeps angles. The test checks every pair of drawn circles, not just a few samples.

What the old page and applet said

The article states that no two Apollonian circles intersect; that is confirmed, but it applies to the first family only — all circles of the second family deliberately meet at A and B. The applet's N spinner runs from 1 to 100 with a default of 5, Family 1 starts on and Family 2 off. Its Reset method was empty, so the Reset points button here is a small convenience, and its red/orange gradients are replaced by two site colours. The live cut-the-knot page no longer embeds the Java applet; an archived capture from 2006 shows APPLET CODE="CoaxalCircles" WIDTH=600 HEIGHT=550 on this same page, which is how the options and formulas above were checked.

Tick Family 2, then drag A and B close together: every green circle still crosses every blue one at a right angle.
